catalog_locator: Appendix D. Introduction and code list pp. 235-236; category I heading p. 236; category II heading 'II Initial main stress, no info on sec stress:' p. 242; entry 'Thalantji (T72): Austin, Peter (1992)..' p. 243.
catalog_quote: [p. 235] This is a list of languages categorised by stress type and annotated with the main descriptive source and some codes denoting special characteristics of the stress pattern in that language. ... Some of the entries have no descriptive source. These must be handled with caution. ... The T-numbers behind the language names are those given to the languages by Norman Tindale in his 1938 survey ... Explanation of codes: C: stress is claimed to be contrastive E: the descriptive source notes many exceptions to the general rule ... M: morphological considerations play a role in stressing ... QS: marginal quantity-sensitivity (only indicated for languages that are QI otherwise) NS: source mentions there is no sec stress US: unclear whether there is secondary stress [p. 242] II Initial main stress, no info on sec stress: ... [p. 243] Payungu (T70): Austin, Peter (1992). A dictionary of Payungu. La Trobe university, Melbourne. ... Thalantji (T72): Austin, Peter (1992). A dictionary of Thalanyji: Western Australia. La Trobe University, Melbourne. Tharrkari (T65): Klokeid, Terry J. (1969). Thargari phonology and morphology. Pacific Linguistics, Series B-12. Canberra.
sweep_summary: Dhalandji/Thalanyji is not in the catalog. Both works with stress in the title (Luján 1986 x2, 'Stress and binding of pronouns') are false hits: the Glottolog records themselves say the language link is a 'computerized assignment from \"binding\"' (an alternate-name string match); they are generative-syntax papers on pronoun stress in English/Spanish and are irrelevant. Hunting beyond the title list, I downloaded and read every open first-hand Austin source on the Kanyara languages (1981 Lingua historical phonology; 1983 PL-A66 dictionaries paper; 1988 PL-A71 classification; 1988 LTUWP voicing survey; 1988 LTUWP Gascoyne-Ashburton survey), Thieberger's 1993 handbook entry, Wikipedia, Wangka Maya's language page and Austin's personal site: none states where Thalanyji word stress falls. The only nearby stress statements are generic (Austin 1988 voicing survey: stops contrast 'usually after the first (stressed) vowel of a word', over languages that exclude Thalanyji) or for a neighbouring Mantharta language (Klokeid 1969 Tharrgari: first vowel after a juncture most strongly stressed). No first-hand Dhalandji stress statement was read, so the best new statement = none. The sources that almost certainly contain one — Deak/Wangka Maya 2008 Thalanyji sketch grammar (155 pp), the 2008 Wangka Maya Thalanyji Dictionary, and Austin's 1992 La Trobe Dictionary of Thalanyji / unpublished Kanyara reference grammar and 'Southern Pilbara phonology' typescript — are print-only or unpublished (priority high; obtain via AIATSIS, Wangka Maya, or Peter Austin directly). (another process was also writing files into that directory during this search of works with stress in the title; I did not read them).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (11,458 lines). Line 10684 reads exactly "II Initial main stress, no info on sec stress:" and sits directly after the running head "242 AUSTRALIAN ABORIGINAL LANGUAGES" (printed p. 242). Lines 10741-10743 read exactly "Thalantji (T72):" / " Austin, Peter (1992). A dictionary of Thalanyji: Western Australia. La" / " Trobe University, Melbourne." and fall after the "APPENDIX D 243" running head (printed p. 243). The entry carries no codes; the Appendix D introduction (txt 10380-10410, pp. 235-236) defines the codes (C contrastive, E many exceptions, M morphological, NS no secondary, US unclear secondary, etc.) and says T-numbers are Tindale's, and warns that some entries were deduced f…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the first syllable of the word (Goedemans's classification of Thalanyji from Austin's 1992 dictionary; no information on secondary stress). Corroborated only by Austin's own regional statement on yinggarda.org (Spelling page, saved): 'In general, stress (emphasis) falls on the first vowel of a word.. The same is true of Bayungu.. and other languages', which the site's Languages-and-people page says applies to all languages of the region including Thalanyji, but the stress sentence does not name Thalanyji.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Goedemans: 'no info on sec stress' (category II). No source examined says anything about secondary stress in Thalanyji.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned (Goedemans marks exceptions with code E; the Thalantji entry carries no codes).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level classification in a typological appendix; no data on phrase-level stress or citation forms. Second-hand: the primary source (Austin 1992 dictionary, 'Guide to orthography and pronunciation' section per Google Books) was not openable; Google Books' full-text index returns that volume for 'Thalanyji'+'stress' and 'Thalanyji'+'first syllable' but shows no pages.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 'Dhalandji' = Thalanyji (AIATSIS W26, Tindale T72 'Thalantji'); Austin 1988 (LTUWP 1) notes Thalanyji is spoken in several dialects differing in vocabulary and phonology, but no source examined names a dialect for the stress claim. Related-language statements held by the project are NOT this language: Klokeid 1969 (Tharrgari, Mantharta, thar1244) and Austin's yinggarda.org/jiwarli.com pages (Yinggarda, Bayungu bayu1240, Jiwarli).

sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: The paper is a generative syntax/semantics study of English focus binding ('Only I got a question that I could answer', 'Only Mary still looks like Mary'); all data are English, with German datives, Navajo and Zazaki/Slave appearing only via cited literature. It contains no phonology and never mentions Thalanyji, Kanyara, or any Australian language. Its listing under dhal1245 is a Glottolog misattribution. The only 'accent' hits in the text (the text) are example sentences about speaking with a foreign accent, not word stress.
